horoscopes.intro: November 16 in the stars: Find out what’s in store for you today in our daily horoscopes for Monday November 16. Read the daily horoscopes for your Sun sign or rising sign (ascendant) to plan your day.

aries.text: Feeling braver than usual this Monday, Aries? The skies are more than happy to support your courageous moves. Action planet Mars meets up with expansive Jupiter in your fifth house of romance, taking a connection from mild to muy picante. Scrap the Victorian playbook and make the first move. Subtle? Not today. Both planets can make you come on strong, though, so warm things up slowly instead of pouncing. This is also a stellar day for creative projects. Post your latest work or pitch an idea you’ve been sitting on. Someone influential could take notice. Already attached? Plan something for tonight that neither of you would call typical.

taurus.text: Anyone who crosses your people today will meet a wall, Taurus. Mars and abundant Jupiter meet in your fourth house of family, putting you in full defense mode, and that protectiveness extends to your own work as well. The catch is that you may not stop to check who’s actually attacking. Before you bare your fangs, consider the source, since a dear friend or relative could be handing you sound advice in a clumsy wrapper.

gemini.text: People will hang on your every word today, Gemini, so choose them wisely. Feisty Mars joins jovial Jupiter in your third house of communication, making you a compelling presence in any room or thread. Use your voice to speak up for a cause and you could raise awareness, maybe even some money. That same firepower works in an argument, though, and no one is likely to outtalk you. Pull your punches if a conversation gets too heated. The snappiest comeback of the day can still do lasting damage to a relationship you’d rather keep.

cancer.text: Guard those purse strings today, Cancer. Money burns a hole in your pocket with impulsive Mars and indulgent Jupiter aligned in your luxuriating second house, leaving you helpless in the face of pretty, shiny things. Do you need it, or do you simply want it very badly at 2PM on a Monday? Start a Pinterest board or a Black Friday wish list instead of buying on impulse. The sales are still three weeks out, so nothing is getting away from you. And if you can’t resist, save the receipt, because this might be one worth returning.

leo.text: You’ve got no filter today, Leo, and you may not want one. Brash Mars syncs up with bloviating Jupiter in your sign, making you irrepressibly candid. You’re simply speaking with passion, though others could read it as confrontation. Is a little pushiness ever warranted? Absolutely. If someone needs a nudge to get moving, don’t back down from your stance. You know it’ll benefit them in the end. Save the full roar for something that deserves it, like a matter you’re fully invested in.

virgo.text: Deep breaths, Virgo. Today’s Mars-Jupiter meetup in your shadowy twelfth house could magnify your worries, so don’t let them send you into a tailspin. Is the situation as dire as the version playing in your head? This is the day to lean on a logical friend who can help you untangle it. This planetary pairing can also stir up old wounds. Healing is a process, so if you need to talk about the hurt again, there’s no shame in it. Pick the friends who won’t tell you to “get over it already.”

libra.text: Friction in the comments section! Today’s scrappy Mars-Jupiter meetup in your teamwork zone makes collaboration both electric and exasperating. With the right people, you’ll feel real possibility, so gather a few of them for a think-tank session and see what shakes out. As for the organizations falling apart at the seams, why stick around? You don’t have to take one for the team, and you never signed up for that role anyway. Opt out today, or give yourself plenty of room so you don’t absorb anyone else’s drama.

scorpio.text: A career quest picks up speed this Monday, Scorpio. Mars meets Jupiter in your ambitious tenth house, so tap into your drive and take action while the week is young. Pushing people a little is fine. Strong-arming them, on the other hand? That’s where things unravel. The downside of this pairing is that its energy can go from motivating to aggressive without much warning. You could win the battle by sheer force and start a cold war in the process. Make the ask, then give people room to say yes on their own schedule.

sagittarius.text: Bigger, stronger, faster! Today’s Mars-Jupiter meetup in your ninth house sounds the call for expansion, and with your ruler involved, you won’t need much convincing. Without risk there’s no reward, Sag. Read the directions and get the lay of the land first, but accept that you’ll make a few mistakes as you stretch and grow. Chalk them up as learning experiences. You’ll never collect any unless you try something new.

capricorn.text: Lust be a Sea Goat tonight! Frisky Mars syncs up with bawdy Jupiter in your seductive eighth house and you’re running hot. The cat-and-mouse routine has been fun, but your patience is wearing thin. How much longer do you plan to hedge before making your desires known? The time has come for your reveal, or at least to be considerably more obvious than you’ve managed so far. The same goes for a business dealing. Put the offer on the table and let them react to a real number instead of a hint.

aquarius.text: Is it getting a little too hot in that kitchen, Aquarius? Today’s Mars-Jupiter merger turns up the flame on your relationships, and you may realize a partnership is moving faster than you’d like. Before you head for the door, make sure you aren’t operating on assumptions. Have you actually asked what the other person expects of you? If they’re reasonable, there should be plenty of room to negotiate, and you might discover the pace is moving along just fine.

pisces.text: Today’s Mars-Jupiter merger could turn you into a raging perfectionist, so stay on high alert. You could fuss over something until midnight, Pisces, only to find another “flaw.” While you like things done just so, think twice if that means losing a night’s sleep or blowing your budget. Who exactly are you trying to impress here? Push too hard and you may wind up intimidating them, or leaving them feeling like they could never measure up. Finish it, send it, and go to bed at a reasonable hour.

items.title: School-Based Health Centers and Student Health Care Use, Need, and Health Outcomes
items.originalTitle: School-Based Health Centers and Student Health Care Use, Need, and Health Outcomes
items.summary: Importance: School-based health centers (SBHCs) are health clinics located in schools that provide comprehensive primary medical care at low or no cost to students.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract:
Importance: School-based health centers (SBHCs) are health clinics located in schools that provide comprehensive primary medical care at low or no cost to students. SBHCs are well positioned to improve health outcomes and health care use by eliminating transportation and cost barriers and to reduce disparities by primarily serving communities with low household incomes and high health care needs.

Objective: To determine the association of SBHC access with health, unmet health care need, and health care receipt for high school students in Oregon.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study used 10 years of student survey data during 2006 to 2023 linked to information on SBHC access in high schools in Oregon. Participants were students in 11th grade statewide who took the health survey. Using entropy-balanced staggered difference-in-differences regressions, we estimated the association of having an SBHC at a student's school with their outcomes. Data analysis was performed from July to September 2026.

Exposure: School-level measure of whether an SBHC was present in a high school in Oregon.

Main outcomes and measures: Three measures of mental health and suicidality, 2 measures of physical health, 2 measures of unmet health care need, and 1 measure of medical care received.

Results: Among 87 871 students at 180 schools, 43 397 (49.7%) were female, 42 824 (49.0%) were male, and 1157 (1.3%) were another gender. A total of 14 933 students attended a school with an SBHC during the study period. SBHC access was associated with statistically significant improvements in student mental health, with decreases in suicidal thoughts (-2.7 percentage points [pp]; 95% CI, -4.5 to -0.7 pp) and suicide attempts (-1.4 pp; 95% CI, -2.3 to -0.5 pp) and decreases in reports of unmet emotional health care needs (-2.1 pp; 95% CI, -3.8 to -0.6 pp). No other statistically significant associations with SBHC access were observed. Heterogeneous treatment effects by gender, sexual orientation, race and ethnicity, and rurality were observed.

Conclusions and relevance: This study found that SBHC access was associated with improved mental health among high school students. There are nearly 4000 SBHCs in the United States, and they are primarily in schools with a high share of students from low-income families. Expanding access to SBHCs may help reduce mental health disparities.

items.abstract:
Importance: Structural inequities stemming from historical redlining and environmental injustice have created varying levels of risk among marginalized communities. However, the association of climate risk and structural racism with pediatric mental health care use remains underexplored.

Objectives: To examine associations between climate vulnerability and pediatric mental health care use, and to assess whether these associations vary by historical redlining status.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study of children aged younger than 18 years residing in New York State between 2017 and 2022 used all-payer hospital administrative data from the New York State Department of Health. Statistical analysis was conducted from January 2025 through February 2026.

Main outcome and measures: Outcomes included mental health-related emergency department (ED) and outpatient visits identified using International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision-coded mental health diagnosis subtypes (eg, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), aggregated at the census-tract level. The primary exposure was climate-specific Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles (where 1 indicates low climate vulnerability and 4 indicates high climate vulnerability). Poisson regression models were conducted to examine associations between Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles and mental health-related health care utilization, including interactions with neighborhood-level redlining status (Home Owners' Loan Corporation grades C/D vs A/B) and subtype-specific analyses. Models adjusted for age, sex, self- or guardian-reported race and ethnicity, and neighborhood-level covariates, with coefficients reported as rate ratios (RRs).

Results: A total of 553 134 mental health-related visits were included (mean [SD] age, 7.2 [5.8] years; 285 526 male [51.6%]). Compared with children living in areas with the lowest climate vulnerability, those living in the highest-vulnerability areas had higher outpatient visit rates (RR, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.72-2.27) and non-statistically significantly higher ED visit rates (RR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.96-1.35). items.title: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
items.originalTitle: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
items.summary: Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. We then generalise the architecture across orthogonal chemical inputs and combinatorial promoters, and combine measured co-culture updates with external game analysis and simulate negative pruning in nonlinear-classifier architectures. These results establish physical learning in living matter through local negative updates of genetically encoded analogue weights.

Importance: Alzheimer disease (AD) pathology can be detected years before symptom onset, but some individuals who are biomarker positive and cognitively unimpaired (CU) remain asymptomatic.

Objective: To estimate 5- and 10-year absolute risks of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia using continuous plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) and p-tau217/amyloid β 42 (Aβ42).

Participants were CU individuals aged 60 to 90 years with baseline Fujirebio Lumipulse plasma p-tau217 measurements, APOE genotyping, and longitudinal clinical follow-up. The MCSA is a population-based longitudinal cohort of residents in Olmsted County, Minnesota; ADNI is a multicenter observational cohort. MCSA data were ascertained from October 2008 to September 2025; ADNI data from September 2005 to January 2026.

Exposures: Age, sex, APOE ε4, p-tau217, and p-tau217/Aβ42.

items.title: Emergence Delirium and Agitation in Older Adults After General Anesthesia: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Evidence Map of Incidence and Perioperative Risk Factors
items.originalTitle: Emergence Delirium and Agitation in Older Adults After General Anesthesia: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Evidence Map of Incidence and Perioperative Risk Factors
items.summary: In recent years, emergence delirium and emergence agitation (ED/EA) have become more clinically significant perioperative brain health phenomena in older adults after a period of early recovery following general anesthesia.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.source: Journal of perianesthesia nursing : official journal of the American Society of PeriAnesthesia Nurses
items.abstract:
Purpose: In recent years, emergence delirium and emergence agitation (ED/EA) have become more clinically significant perioperative brain health phenomena in older adults after a period of early recovery following general anesthesia. Nevertheless, the existing evidence on ED/EA remains fragmented across different definitions, and the role of modifiable perioperative factors remains incompletely defined. We aimed to estimate the incidence of ED/EA in elderly people after general anesthesia, synthesize the adjusted risk-factor evidence, and identify the clinically relevant perioperative domain.

Design: The systematic review and meta-analysis.

Methods: Searches in PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and Embase were performed from inception to April 30, 2026. Eligible studies enrolled older surgical patients undergoing general anesthesia and reported ED, PACU delirium, or emergence agitation during emergence or PACU stay. Incidence was pooled using logit-transformed random-effects models. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were pooled when at least two clinically comparable estimates were available; heterogeneous or single-study factors were summarized by evidence mapping.

Findings: Twelve reports representing eight independent cohorts or study populations were included. The main incidence analysis included seven independent cohorts with 3601 patients and 1161 ED/EA events, yielding a pooled incidence of 29.7% (95% CI: 23.4%-36.8%). Increasing age (OR = 1.07 per year, 95% CI: 1.04-1.10) and higher early recovery pain score were the most reproducible risk signals. In the NRS-only sensitivity analysis, each one-point increase in pain score was associated with a 29% higher risk of ED/EA (OR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.21-1.37), with no observed heterogeneity. Nutritional risk, hypothermia, catheter-related discomfort, urinary catheterization, preoperative anxiety, and selected anesthetic or non-pharmacological interventions emerged as clinically relevant but insufficiently homogeneous candidate factors.

Conclusions: ED/EA affects approximately one-third of older adults during early recovery after general anesthesia. Current reproducible evidence supports age and early recovery pain as stable risk indicators, while evidence mapping highlights nutrition, temperature management, catheter-related factors and perioperative comfort as promising targets for future prospective prevention studies.

items.title: Interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality: a global systematic review
items.originalTitle: Interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality: a global systematic review
items.summary: Perinatal suicidality (suicidal thoughts, behaviours, plans and attempts) is a risk factor for suicide. Evidence on interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality remains limited. This systematic review examined the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions to reduce suicidality in perinatal women.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.source: Journal of reproductive and infant psychology
items.abstract:
Introduction: Perinatal suicidality (suicidal thoughts, behaviours, plans and attempts) is a risk factor for suicide. Evidence on interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality remains limited. This systematic review examined the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions to reduce suicidality in perinatal women.

Methods: This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251081528). Seven databases were searched from 2010 to December 2025. Interventions assessing a reduction in perinatal suicidality as a primary, secondary, or safety monitoring outcome were included. Two reviewers independently screened articles. A narrative summary was compiled. Risk of bias was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.

Results: Six studies were included: 5 randomised controlled trials (3 individually randomised, 1 cluster, 1 noninferiority) and 1 historical controlled trial. Three studies investigated suicidality as a primary or secondary outcome, and three studies collected suicidality data for safety monitoring. Of these, two investigated multidisciplinary community health programmes, and one evaluated a behavioural activation therapy. Two studies showed a reduction in suicidality, and one showed a significant reduction at 3-4 months postpartum, but not at 7-8 months. Three studies assessed suicidality as safety monitoring. These studies investigated eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing therapy, a practice-level intervention incorporated into obstetric practices, and an electronic mindfulness-based intervention. These studies were not adequately powered to assess a reduction in suicidality.

Discussion: Few studies have investigated suicidality as a primary or secondary outcome. Although some health system level and psychological interventions were associated with a reduction in suicidality, robust evidence from interventions specifically designed to reduce perinatal suicidality is needed.

items.title: Design Strategies in Discrete Choice Experiments for Individuals with Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review
items.originalTitle: Design Strategies in Discrete Choice Experiments for Individuals with Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review
items.summary: Patient preference evidence is increasingly important for value assessment and decision making in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Discrete choice experiments (DCEs) are widely used to elicit patient preferences but may raise feasibility concerns in individuals with cognitive impairment.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Objectives: Patient preference evidence is increasingly important for value assessment and decision making in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Discrete choice experiments (DCEs) are widely used to elicit patient preferences but may raise feasibility concerns in individuals with cognitive impairment. We aimed to systematically review studies that explicitly evaluated design choices in DCEs for preference elicitation in individuals with cognitive impairment.

Methods: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL/PsycINFO through January 23, 2026 for studies that evaluated DCE design adaptations or feasibility in cognitively impaired populations. Findings were synthesized narratively according to adaptations and their reported effects on comprehension, task performance, and respondent burden.

Results: We identified six studies. Four categories of design adaptations were identified: attribute description, simplification of choice task structure, visual design and layout, and survey administration. We learned that attribute familiarity and concreteness improved understanding; respondents struggled when the status-quo state was not anchored to their own current health state. Limiting to three options per task and three attributes per option improved completion rates. Greater overlap in attribute levels across options made tasks easier to complete. Use of icons as illustrations improved attribute comprehension, and caregiver involvement in interviewer-administered surveys aided completion.

Conclusions: Existing evidence suggests that DCEs can be successfully completed by individuals with mild cognitive impairment or early-stage dementia when tasks are appropriately adapted to lessen complexity. However, the evidence base remains limited. Additional methodological research is needed to identify design strategies that improve accessibility of these tasks to those with cognitive challenges while generating meaningful preference information.

items.title: Simultaneous EEG-fMRI in major depressive disorder: A systematic review of brain networks, neurovascular coupling, and clinical correlates
items.originalTitle: Simultaneous EEG-fMRI in major depressive disorder: A systematic review of brain networks, neurovascular coupling, and clinical correlates
items.summary: Simultaneous electroencephalography-functional magnetic resonance imaging (EEG-fMRI) offers unique potential to characterize brain network dysfunction and neurovascular coupling in major depressive disorder (MDD).
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Background: Simultaneous electroencephalography-functional magnetic resonance imaging (EEG-fMRI) offers unique potential to characterize brain network dysfunction and neurovascular coupling in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the field lacks a rigorous synthesis restricted to strictly defined MDD populations with true multimodal integration.

Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420261292902), we searched PubMed, Scopus, CENTRAL, and Google Scholar (inception to March 2026) for simultaneous EEG-fMRI studies in adults (≥18 years) with MDD. We excluded subclinical samples, healthy-only populations, and sequential acquisitions to ensure diagnostic specificity. Primary outcomes were network dysfunction, neurovascular coupling, and clinical associations. Narrative synthesis was performed due to data paucity (<3 studies/outcome). Risk of bias was assessed using modified ROB2, ROBINS-I, and JBI tools.

Results: Nine studies (eight cohorts; N=377) met strict criteria. Two reports from one cohort investigating anhedonia via neurofeedback (Zotev et al.) showed moderate-to-strong correlations between EEG-fMRI metrics and severity (r = 0.47 and 0.69). Single-study findings reported effect sizes for anxiety (r = 0.74), depression change (r = -0.38 to 0.90), and rumination (r = 0.20). Analytical heterogeneity was substantial. Evidence certainty was low due to bias risk and imprecision.

Limitations: Small sample sizes, methodological fragmentation, and reliance on single cohorts for specific outcomes limit generalizability.

Conclusions: Simultaneous EEG-fMRI identifies strong neurophysiological correlates (e.g., anhedonia, treatment response) in active contexts (e.g., neurofeedback, ketamine), but evidence for generalizable resting-state biomarkers remains insufficient. Future efforts must prioritize standardized pipelines and large-scale cohorts to transition this technique to a clinical biomarker.

items.title: The prevalence of dementia and cognitive impairment in patients with neurocysticercosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.originalTitle: The prevalence of dementia and cognitive impairment in patients with neurocysticercosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is a leading parasitic infection of the central nervous system and an important cause of neurological morbidity in endemic regions. Although seizures are well-characterized manifestations, the burden of cognitive impairment and dementia in NCC remains poorly quantified.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Background: Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is a leading parasitic infection of the central nervous system and an important cause of neurological morbidity in endemic regions. Although seizures are well-characterized manifestations, the burden of cognitive impairment and dementia in NCC remains poorly quantified. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia among patients with NCC and to explore sources of between-study variability.

Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar (June-July 2025) and registered the protocol in PROSPERO (CRD420251106614). Observational studies reporting dementia or cognitive impairment in imaging-confirmed NCC were eligible. Data extraction and quality assessment were independently performed, and risk of bias was evaluated using the Hoy tool. Pooled prevalence estimates were generated using random-effects models with REML and Hartung-Knapp adjustments. Exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) confidence intervals and logit-transformations were applied. Prespecified subgroup, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses assessed heterogeneity.

Results: Nine studies met inclusion criteria (N = 798 for cognitive impairment; N = 296 for dementia). The pooled prevalence of cognitive impairment was 50% (95% CI: 0.23-0.76; I²=97.87%) and dementia 10% (95% CI: 0.05-0.15; I²=49.11%). Subgroup analyses showed significant regional variation, with highest cognitive impairment prevalence in South America (68%). Cognitive assessment method did not account for heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of pooled estimates, and no significant small-study effects were detected.

Conclusion: Cognitive impairment affects approximately half of patients with NCC, while one in ten develop dementia. Geographic context and methodological factors largely drive between-study variability. These findings underscore NCC as an important contributor to neurocognitive morbidity in endemic regions and highlight the need for standardized cognitive assessment, harmonized diagnostic criteria, and longitudinal studies to clarify disease mechanisms and progression.
